How to Measure the Distance?
We cannot use brightness
● Brightness depends on size and temperature as well
We cannot just go there
● It would take too long (but see proposed “Project Starshot”)
Distance determination is one of the hardest problems in 
observational astronomy
The best solution: Parallax
● Only works for nearby stars
● Familiar idea, but maybe not a familiar name…

Parallax in Astronomy
Based on the same idea
● Measure apparent motion of nearby stars
We cannot use our eyes
● Need a longer base-line (a bigger separation between viewpoints)
● What can we do?

Annual Parallax
The trick to stellar parallax
● Use the Earth’s motion around the Sun
● Baseline of 2AU (300 million km)
The trouble with this
● The measurement takes at least six 
months
● Stars also move, mimicking parallax
● Need to repeat over a few years to tell 
the difference between parallax and 
stellar motion

In Class Demo: Understanding Parallax 
1. Close left eye
2. Line up finger with me
3. Keep the finger in the same place, but switch eyes
4. How much does the finger appear to move relative to me?
5. Now repeat the experiment with the finger at arms length
This is parallax
● Nearby things appear to move 
more when you switch eyes
● This is how you judge distances

The Limits of Parallax
All stars have parallax less than 1 arcsec
● Really tough to measure
From the ground cannot do better than 0.01arcsec
● Limiting distance is 1/0.01=100pc
From space, you can do better (no atmosphere to blur things)
● E.g. European satellite Hipparcos could do 0.001 arcsec
● Can do 100’s of parsecs
The Galaxy is around 50,000 parsec diameter!
● For most of Galaxy distance determination is tricky business

Stellar Luminosities and Brightnesses
The luminosity of a star is really important
● For the Sun, luminosity told us rate of nuclear fusion
● We estimated how long the Sun’s fuel could last
For the stars we can work it out:
● How bright are they?
● How distant are they? (ideally parallax)
✦b = brightness (W/m2)
✦L = luminosity (W)
✦d = distance (m)
✦This is the “inverse square law” - brightness varies inversely with distance 
squared

● Distance = 150 million km = 1.5x1011m
Sirius

● Distance = 8.61 light years = 8.15x1016m

Flux, Luminosity, and Brightness
Flux
● Power emerging from 1m2 of a star’s surface
● Given by Stefan-Boltzmann Law
● Abbreviated to F
● Sometimes called surface brightness
Luminosity
● Total power emerging from star’s surface
● Flux x surface area
● Abbreviated to L
● Independent of distance
Brightness
● Power crossing 1m2 at Earth
● e.g. light collected by a 1m2 area telescope
● Abbreviated to b
● Diminishes with distance: Luminosity ÷ (distance)2
● Do not confuse with ‘surface brightness’

Apparent vs Absolute magnitude
The magnitude of a star as we measure it here on Earth is called 
“Apparent magnitude” (denoted with small “m”)
● Low magnitudes are brighter
● Depends on distance, temperature etc
The “real” magnitude of a star if we could measure it from a 
distance of 10pc is called “Absolute magnitude” (denoted with 
capital “M”)
● Conveys measure of true brightness of a star
● Independent of distance

How are Luminous Stars Different to the Sun?
Nothing to do with distance
● Luminosity is energy output, not apparent brightness
Partly temperature
● Stefan-Boltzmann Law - hotter stars are more luminous
● E.g. Sirius is hotter than the Sun (~10,000K) and more luminous
Not just temperature
● E.g. Betelgeuse has luminosity 41,000 L, but is cooler than the Sun 
(3100K)
● Why?  Betelgeuse is much larger - it is a “supergiant”

✦Total area = 4R2
● Total luminosity = 4R2 x T4

The Interstellar Medium
The space between the stars is not a vacuum
● It contains low density gas and dust
● Gas can produce absorption or emission lines (Kirchhoff’s Laws)

Red Giants

As the Sun ages helium builds up in core
 ● At some point all hydrogen in core exhausted
 ● Pressure drops, core contracts, releases more heat
 ● Now hydrogen around core is hot enough to burn - shell-burning

But now the thermostat is faulty
 ● Shell burning does not stop contraction of core
 ● This gets hotter, over-heating shell-burning layer
 ● Reaction rate increases
   (CNO cycle takes over)
 ● Luminosity dramatically increases
 ● Star expands to radiate
   away excess luminosity
 ● Expansion cools envelope -
   star becomes cooler

Say that again…?

As the core contracts it makes the envelope expand and cool
 ● This is not very intuitive!
 ● Recurrent theme in stellar evolution
    ✦ Burning in core  normal core, compact hot star
    ✦ Burning in shell  dense core, huge cool star

Complex situation, no simple explanation
 ● ‘the transition from main sequence to giant branch involves a
   complicated interplay between a core, an envelope, and a nuclear-
   burning shell, and a “simple explanation” as to how this interplay
   causes stars to become giants can be an inappropriate and
   misleading description of a complex situation’ - Icko Iben, 1993, in
   The Astrophysical Journal

Accretion Disks

       First star evolves, sheds its envelope, leaves behind a white dwarf.

Then the second star that was originally the less massive evolves, fills its Roche

homework.prompt: Which nebula from the list below has the highest gas density?
homework.explanation: Among the offered planetary, reflection, dark and emission nebulae, the course key selects the dense dark cloud.

homework.prompt: In reflection nebulae, the characteristic blue color is due to:
homework.answerText: The scattering of ultra-violet background star light in interstellar dust
homework.displayedKey: Scattering of ultra-violet background starlight in interstellar dust
homework.explanation: This is the displayed homework key. Lecture 30 page 13 instead says scattering of blue light. Learn dust scattering as the mechanism; the wavelength wording conflicts.

homework.topic: Binaries/multiple systems usually form within Bok globules
homework.prompt: Binary and multiple star systems are usually formed within Bok Globules.
homework.explanation: The course connects dense star-forming clouds with binary and multiple-star formation.

homework.prompt: During the giant star phase of stellar evolution, nuclear burning occurs:
homework.answerText: In the hydrogen-burning shell around the helium core
homework.explanation: This describes the first red-giant stage. Later giant stages have different burning regions.

homework.topic: Helium flash creates clear outward signal
homework.prompt: After the ‘helium flash’ signifying the start of core helium burning in a giant star, there is a clear outward signal that can be seen emerging from the star.
homework.explanation: The core flash is not a directly visible surface explosion; the envelope absorbs and redistributes the energy.

homework.prompt: A star has a mass of 100 times the mass of the sun and a luminosity of 1,000,000 that of the sun. How long will the star live in the main-sequence? Provide your answer in units of years. Hint: Take the main-sequence life-time of the sun to be 10 billion years (10^10 years).
homework.explanation: Lifetime scales as fuel divided by consumption rate: 10¹⁰ × 100 / 1,000,000 = 10⁶ years.

homework.topic: Evolution stages matched to main energy source
homework.prompt: Match the evolutionary stages of sun-like stars with their corresponding main source of energy.
homework.answerText: AGB → helium burning in a shell around the core; main sequence → hydrogen burning in the core; red giant → hydrogen burning in a shell around the core; horizontal branch → helium burning in the core; protostar → gravitational contraction; white dwarf → none.
homework.displayedKey: AGB: helium shell; main sequence: core hydrogen; red giant: hydrogen shell; horizontal branch: core helium; protostar: contraction; white dwarf: none
homework.explanation: ‘None’ means no ongoing nuclear burning, not zero luminosity. An AGB star can also have a hydrogen-burning shell; the supplied matching key emphasizes its helium shell.

homework.prompt: During the Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stage the core of star is made of helium.
homework.explanation: The AGB core is carbon/oxygen; helium burning occurs in a surrounding shell.

homework.prompt: The reason that the shape of many planetary nebula appears to be ‘bipolar’ could be due to: Hint: There might be more than 1 right answer.
homework.answerText: a and d: interaction in a binary star system; material concentrated in an equatorial disk, channeling gas toward the polar directions.
homework.displayedKey: Binary gravitational interaction AND equatorial disk channeling gas poleward
homework.explanation: The explicit complete key gives these two explanations. Rapid rotation disrupting the outflow (option c) is not part of that key.

homework.topic: Observation supporting iron core-collapse supernova mechanism
homework.prompt: What discovery confirmed the theory of ‘iron core-collapse’ as the mechanism that drives supernova explosions?
homework.answerText: The discovery of supernova neutrinos in SN1987A
homework.explanation: Neutrinos provide direct evidence of the collapse event, beyond the later optical brightening.

homework.prompt: A nearby supernova could have catastrophic consequences for life on Earth because:
homework.answerText: Energetic gamma-rays and X-rays destroy the ozone layer, exposing Earth’s ecosystem to lethal UV radiation from the Sun.
homework.displayedKey: Gamma/X rays destroy ozone, exposing life to solar UV
homework.explanation: The course mechanism is atmospheric damage followed by increased solar ultraviolet exposure.

homework.topic: Nickel/cobalt decay powers late supernova light
homework.prompt: Radioactive decay of unstable heavier elements like nickel and cobalt is the source of energy that powers the light from a supernova for years after the explosion.
homework.explanation: The nickel → cobalt → iron decay chain can power the later light curve; this is distinct from the collapse energy and the initial shock.

homework.prompt: Which expression below best describes gravity in the context of Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity?
homework.answerText: Matter causes space to curve; space causes matter to move.
homework.displayedKey: Matter causes space to curve; space causes matter to move
homework.explanation: Mass-energy curves spacetime, and freely moving objects follow paths set by that geometry.

homework.topic: Short GRBs caused by massive rotating star collapse
homework.prompt: Short-duration Gamma Ray Bursts are caused by the collapse of a massive rotating star.
homework.explanation: The course associates massive-star collapse with long bursts and compact-object mergers with short bursts.

homework.prompt: Light passing near the vicinity of a black hole will:
homework.answerText: Bend due to the curvature of space around the black hole and change direction due to the gravitational lensing effect.
homework.displayedKey: Bends because of curvature / gravitational lensing
homework.explanation: Passing near a black hole is different from crossing the event horizon. Deflection does not require capture.
